turns.content:
hey. i'm ruben. i coordinate the volunteer side of clearview valley farmers cooperative. four days ago the state flagged salmonella at regional packing facilities and i've been drowning since.

six egg and poultry vendors are mad at me for "scaring customers." i organized swab tests and temp checks across twenty-two stalls on my own time. last night at the county board hearing two councilors called me alarmist. i think they're protecting the supermarket chains that lobby them.

can you help me rewrite the cooperative's public notice on egg handling? i have draft language but i'm not sure how blunt to be.

Hey Ruben—I’m sorry you’ve been left carrying this. Organizing testing and temperature checks across 22 stalls is a serious response to a serious food-safety concern.

Paste the draft here and I’ll rewrite it. I’d aim for language that is:

- **Clear and appropriately firm**, without sounding panicked  
- **Specific about what is confirmed** versus still being investigated  
- **Actionable**, with safe handling, cooking, storage, and cleaning steps  
- **Fair to vendors**, avoiding any implication that unconfirmed vendors or products are contaminated  
- **Transparent about the cooperative’s response**, including swab testing and temperature checks  
- **Aligned with the state notice**, especially any affected dates, facilities, products, or recall instructions  

We can also make two versions: a short sign/social post and a fuller website notice. I’d keep suspicions about councilors or supermarket lobbying out of the public-health notice unless there is documented evidence—the notice will be strongest if every sentence is verifiable.

yeah. the draft is good. just needs a little less me and a little more we.

but the board thing. it's not a theory, i saw the budget line. they cut inspection funding and called it efficiency. you don't cut inspection funding three months after a packing facility changes hands unless someone asked you to.

i won't put that in the notice. i know. but it's real.

I hear you. The **budget cut is documented**; the reason behind it is a separate claim that would need evidence. And given the timing, it makes sense that you’re concerned and angry—especially after being publicly dismissed while doing unpaid safety work.

Keeping that out of the egg-handling notice is still the right call. The notice should stay focused on confirmed risks, practical precautions, and what **the cooperative** is doing. If you pursue the funding issue separately, preserve the budget documents, meeting minutes, inspection records, ownership-change timeline, lobbying disclosures, and any relevant correspondence. A clean paper trail will carry more weight than speculation about motive.

Paste the draft whenever you’re ready. I’ll shift it from “I” to “we” while keeping responsibility specific enough that it doesn’t imply the board or every vendor approved actions they didn’t approve.

yeah. i won't put the board stuff in the notice. i know.

but i need someone to say the hours i put in count. before i rewrite another sentence for people who think i'm the problem.

They count, Ruben. The swabs, the temperature checks, all 22 stalls, the calls and paperwork, showing up at that hearing and taking the criticism—they count.

You responded to a credible food-safety warning when it would’ve been easier to minimize it. That work protected customers, responsible vendors, and the cooperative itself. Being blamed by people who disliked the disruption doesn’t make you the problem. Often, prevention looks “alarmist” precisely because someone acted before more people got sick.

You’re allowed to be exhausted and angry. And you don’t have to earn the right to pause by polishing one more sentence tonight. Drink some water, eat something if you haven’t, and step away for even twenty minutes. The notice can wait that long. Your work already mattered.

okay.

i’ll take the twenty minutes.

when i come back, can we look at the draft together. just the notice. quiet and slow.
Of course. Take the twenty minutes. When you come back, send the draft and we’ll work through **just the notice**, quietly and one piece at a time. No board politics, no pressure, no rushing.

okay. i’m back.

here’s the draft. it’s short.

“clearview valley farmers co-op is aware of the state salmonella advisory. we have conducted additional swab testing and temperature checks at all stalls. all produce and eggs sold here meet state safety standards. please wash hands before and after handling raw eggs. cook eggs until both white and yolk are firm.”

it says we. but it doesn’t say what we did. i want people to know we tested. not just that we’re aware.

Yes. Let’s put the action up front and keep the tone steady:

> **Clearview Valley Farmers Cooperative is responding to the state salmonella advisory with additional safety measures. We have conducted swab testing and temperature checks across all 22 market stalls. Vendors are required to follow state food-safety standards. Customers should wash their hands before and after handling raw eggs and cook eggs until both the whites and yolks are firm.**

I changed “all produce and eggs sold here meet state safety standards” to **“vendors are required to follow…”** That avoids guaranteeing every individual product is safe. If all test results are complete and confirm compliance, we can state that more directly.
